title: Solve it together: the best jump
idea: GUIDED PROBLEM via UEPCC. Choose and apply the MAX pattern to find the longest jump.
problem: Long-jump distances are [4, 7, 5, 6]. What was the best (longest) jump?

exercises.prompt:
PROBLEM: jumps [4, 7, 5, 6]. What was the best (longest) jump?

Understand. What is the OUTPUT?
exercises.explanation: 'Best/longest' is the single biggest value — the max pattern. Name the output first.
The input is the list of distances; you will walk it keeping the best so far.

exercises.prompt: Example by hand. Scan [4, 7, 5, 6] keeping the best so far. What is the longest?
exercises.explanation: best goes 4 -> 7, and 5 and 6 never beat 7. The longest jump is 7 — your check value.

options: Max — keep a best-so-far, replace when bigger
exercises.explanation: 'Biggest/longest/best' is the MAX pattern: a best-so-far replaced on a bigger value.
Start at the first real value so the comparison works for any numbers, even negatives.

exercises.prompt: Code it. Arrange the lines to find the longest jump.
exercises.explanation: Start best at the first jump, loop, replace when bigger, print. Mirrors the plan.
Replace best only when the jump is bigger, so the sign is >.

exercises.prompt: Check. The code prints 7. Your hand example said 7. So...
options: It passes — output matches the example
exercises.explanation: Output matches the hand-found best, so the max solution is correct.

exercises.prompt: New input: jumps = [9, 2, 9, 3]. With the same code, what prints?
exercises.explanation: The best is 9 (it appears twice). Max reports the single biggest value.

exercises.prompt: If you had used < instead of > by mistake, this would have found the SHORTEST jump, not the longest.
exercises.explanation: The comparison sign decides the job. > finds the biggest; < would find the smallest.
